people.biography: A thinker from Miletus in ancient Ionia, Thales was later remembered as an early exponent of explanations based on nature rather than myth. Most accounts of his life were written much later; stories such as his prediction of an eclipse remain disputed. He is included here as a precursor of natural philosophy.
contributions: Sought a common natural principle with which to explain the world.
Later writers credited him with observations of magnets attracting iron, an early episode in the history of magnetism.
notes: His life and attributed discoveries are known mainly from later testimony; the birth and death years are estimates.
He is included as a precursor of natural philosophy; ancient explanations must not be equated with modern experimental theories.

people.biography: Mozi was a Chinese thinker of the Warring States period and the founder of the Mohist school. He valued practical techniques and reasoned argument. The surviving Mozi contains material from different periods: its technical discussions of optics, mechanics and geometry in the Mohist Canons largely belong to later Mohists, rather than to Mozi alone.
contributions: His school preserved early Chinese discussions of shadows, reflection and pinhole images.
Mohist writings examined force, motion, balance and space, providing important evidence for the history of Chinese physical thought.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Mohist Canons

notes: The optical and mechanical discussions in the Mohist Canons are collective achievements of later Mohists and must not all be attributed to Mozi personally.
The birth and death years are disputed estimates; this archive uses approximately 470–391 BCE.

people.biography: A thinker from Abdera in ancient Greece, Democritus developed atomism with Leucippus. Most of his writings are lost, and his views must be reconstructed from later quotations. His account of atoms and void was a natural-philosophical hypothesis, rather than the experimentally established atomic physics of modern science.
contributions: Explained matter and its changes in terms of atoms and void.
Related observable properties to the arrangement and structure of microscopic constituents, supplying a historical resource for later corpuscular theories.
notes: The dates are conventional estimates; ancient atomism differs from modern atomic physics.

people.biography: The Greek philosopher Aristotle studied in Athens and later founded the Lyceum. He wrote extensively on nature, animals and logic. His physics treated motion, change and causes within a systematic framework that shaped ancient and medieval scholarship, while also becoming a central target of early modern scientific criticism.
contributions: Systematically discussed motion, time, place and causal explanation in the Physics.
Developed a distinction between terrestrial and celestial nature that influenced natural philosophy in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries.

people.biography: Euclid was a mathematician active in ancient Alexandria whose life is poorly documented. His Elements supplied a lasting language of geometrical proof for physical theories. His Optics organized questions about vision and perspective into geometrical propositions and belongs to the ancient tradition of mathematical approaches to nature.
contributions: Organized geometry into an axiomatic, deductive system used in mechanics, astronomy and optics.
Used geometry in the Optics to investigate visual angles, lines of sight and apparent size.
notes: Biographical evidence is extremely limited, and reconstructions of his approximate dates differ.

people.biography: An ancient Greek astronomer from Samos, Aristarchus attempted to estimate the relative sizes and distances of the Sun and Moon geometrically. He also proposed a Sun-centred system in which Earth moves around the Sun. This cosmological proposal is known principally through the testimony of Archimedes and other writers.
contributions: Proposed an ancient heliocentric model that used Earth's motion to explain celestial phenomena.
Used lunar phases and angular relationships to estimate relative celestial distances and sizes.

people.biography: Archimedes was a mathematician, engineer and investigator of mechanics in Syracuse. He communicated with scholars in Alexandria and combined rigorous geometrical demonstrations with mechanical reasoning. His work addressed equilibrium, floating bodies and machines. He was killed when Roman forces captured Syracuse.
contributions: Developed mathematical treatments of levers and centres of gravity, advancing statics.
Established principles of buoyancy and equilibrium in On Floating Bodies, a foundational work of hydrostatics.
Used mechanical reasoning to assist geometrical quadrature and investigated devices such as the water-raising screw.

people.biography: Hipparchus was an ancient Greek astronomer associated with Nicaea and Rhodes. He assembled observations and developed quantitative models of solar and lunar motion. Most of his works are lost, but results preserved by Ptolemy and other authors became important foundations for positional astronomy.
contributions: Recognized the precession of the equinoxes by comparing stellar positions from different periods.
Developed trigonometric computation and models that improved quantitative descriptions of celestial positions and periods.

people.biography: Hero, or Heron, was a mathematical and engineering author of ancient Alexandria whose exact dates remain disputed. His writings assembled and developed knowledge of pneumatics, automata, surveying and mechanics, linking Greek mathematical traditions to later engineering practice. The dates in this archive are conventional estimates.
contributions: Described devices operated by air, steam and liquid pressure in the Pneumatica.
Recorded the aeolipile, a reaction-driven rotating device, and discussed mechanisms, equilibrium and measurement.

people.biography: Zhang Heng was a scientist, writer and official of China's Eastern Han dynasty. As an imperial astronomer he worked on calendars and astronomical instruments. He combined mechanical construction with astronomical observation. His earthquake-detecting instrument is described in historical texts, but the original is lost and its internal mechanism remains debated.
contributions: Constructed a water-powered armillary sphere to demonstrate celestial motions.
Created an instrument intended to indicate the direction of distant earthquakes through a mechanical response, an important episode in the history of seismological instruments.

people.biography: Ptolemy was an astronomer, geographer and author on optics active in Alexandria under Roman rule. His Almagest systematized geocentric astronomy, and its models were used for centuries to calculate celestial positions. His Optics preserved quantitative investigations of vision, reflection and refraction.
contributions: Organized mathematical models of planetary positions using devices such as epicycles and eccentric circles.
Investigated reflection and refraction with experimental measurements, advancing ancient geometrical optics.
notes: Sources give birth dates around 85 or 100 CE and death dates around 165 or 170 CE; these ranges are retained.

people.biography: Hypatia was a mathematician, teacher of astronomy and Neoplatonic philosopher in late antique Alexandria, and the daughter of Theon. She taught mathematics and philosophy and helped transmit astronomical learning. Her works and life must largely be reconstructed from later testimony. She was murdered by a mob in 415.
contributions: Taught and transmitted mathematics used in astronomical calculation.
Letters associated with her scholarly circle document knowledge of instruments such as astrolabes and hydrometers, without establishing that she invented them.
notes: Birth is commonly estimated around 355 or 370; she died in March 415, without a securely established exact day.
References in students’ letters do not establish that Hypatia invented the astrolabe or hydrometer.

people.biography: Aryabhata was an Indian mathematician and astronomer best known for the Aryabhatiya, written in 499. His birthplace is disputed. He applied mathematical computation to celestial periods, eclipses and Earth's motion and became a major figure in Indian mathematical astronomy. His exact death date is unknown.
contributions: Explained the apparent daily motion of the stars through Earth's rotation.
Explained eclipses through the shadows of Earth and Moon and developed computational methods for celestial positions.
notes: The birth year is inferred mainly from an age statement in his work; 550 is a conventional approximate death year, not an established exact date.

people.biography: John Philoponus was a late antique Alexandrian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle, educated under Ammonius. He criticized inherited accounts of motion and the cosmos through argument and experience. His writings reached later natural philosophy through Syriac, Arabic and Latin traditions.
contributions: Criticized accounts in which a projectile is continually pushed by the surrounding medium and discussed an imparted capacity for motion.
Challenged a strict proportionality between falling speed and weight and considered the possibility of motion in a vacuum.

people.biography: Brahmagupta was an Indian mathematician and astronomer associated with the Ujjain tradition who composed the Brahmasphutasiddhanta in 628. Alongside numerical methods, he treated celestial calculation, eclipses and instruments, applying mathematics to practical astronomical questions. His death year is only approximate.
contributions: Developed calculations for celestial longitudes, eclipses and conjunctions.
Investigated spherical astronomy and observational instruments, extending Indian quantitative astronomy.
notes: Birth is usually dated 598; death is variously estimated around 668 or 670.

people.biography: Ibn Sahl was a tenth-century mathematician and optical investigator active in Baghdad. Little is known securely about his life, birthplace or cultural identity. contributions: Used a geometrical relation equivalent to the sine law of refraction in lens design.
Analyzed focusing by curved mirrors and lenses and constructed lens shapes intended to reduce geometrical aberration.

people.biography: Al-Biruni was a polymath from Khwarazm whose studies encompassed astronomy, geography, mathematics and natural phenomena. people.biography: Shen Kuo was a Northern Song scientist and official involved in astronomy, calendars, engineering and military affairs. Late in life he compiled the Dream Pool Essays, recording observations, experiments and technical knowledge. Its discussions of astronomy, magnetism, optics and geology are major evidence for the history of Song science.
contributions: Recorded the preparation and use of magnetized needles and described the difference between magnetic north and true north.

people.biography: Witelo was a thirteenth-century scholar active in Silesia and Italy whose exact dates and parts of his life are disputed. His ten-book Perspectiva organized knowledge of vision, reflection and refraction, transmitting Ibn al-Haytham's research to Latin scholarship and later influencing Kepler's optics.
contributions: Systematized geometrical treatments of reflection, refraction and vision.
Transmitted Arabic optical research through the Latin Perspectiva, providing important material for later studies of vision and imaging.

people.biography: Theodoric, or Dietrich, of Freiberg was a German Dominican scholar who studied in Paris and held offices in his order. He investigated knowledge, natural philosophy and optics and analyzed the rainbow through experiment and geometry. His exact birth and death years are not established.
contributions: Used models such as water-filled glass spheres to analyze refraction and internal reflection in primary and secondary rainbows.
Connected ray paths in individual droplets to the rainbow seen by an observer, advancing its quantitative explanation.

contributions: Explained primary and secondary rainbows through refraction and internal reflection in spherical water drops.
Extended Ibn al-Haytham's optical tradition through experimental models and geometrical analysis.

people.biography: Jean Buridan was a fourteenth-century French scholastic philosopher who taught for many years at the University of Paris and served twice as rector. Working within the Aristotelian tradition, he developed impetus as an explanation for a projectile's continued motion after release. His dates can only be estimated.
contributions: Developed and disseminated impetus theory, explaining continued projectile motion through an acquired internal motive quality.
Discussed relationships between impetus, quantity of matter, speed and resistance, leaving important questions for later theories of motion.

He worked on mathematics, economics and natural philosophy and translated Aristotle. His geometrical representations of changing intensities and motion were important intellectual resources before early modern kinematics.
contributions: Used diagrams to represent quantities varying with position or time and investigated uniformly changing motion and the mean-speed relation.
Considered the possibility of Earth's rotation and investigated light and vision.

people.biography: Copernicus was a Polish astronomer educated in Krakow and Italy who later held a church office in Frombork while pursuing astronomical calculations. His On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, published in 1543, rearranged the roles of the Sun, Earth and planets and helped transform European astronomy and natural philosophy.
contributions: Constructed a mathematical heliocentric planetary system using Earth's revolution and rotation to explain celestial appearances.
Explained apparent planetary retrograde motion through Earth's motion, providing a new framework for Kepler and Newton.

Examined relationships between firing angle and range, helping develop quantitative approaches to artillery.

He investigated falling bodies, statics and geometry and criticized Aristotelian explanations of falling speed. His arguments are important evidence for changes in theories of motion before Galileo.

Applied statics and geometrical reasoning to problems of motion and mechanical equilibrium.

people.biography: William Gilbert was an English physician and natural investigator who served as a royal doctor. His De magnete of 1600 distinguished magnetism from frictional electrification through extensive experiments. Using a spherical lodestone as a model of Earth, he became a central figure in the development of experimental magnetism.

Systematically investigated lodestones and frictional electrification and distinguished electrical from magnetic effects.

people.biography: Tycho Brahe was a Danish astronomer who established observatories on the island of Hven and later worked in Prague. Used observations of a new star and comets to challenge the traditional view of an unchanging celestial realm.

people.biography: Harriot was an English mathematician, astronomer and investigator of navigation who served Raleigh and the Earl of Northumberland and joined a colonial expedition to North America. He studied refraction, ballistics and celestial objects, leaving extensive unpublished manuscripts. His telescopic lunar sketches predated Galileo's published lunar observations.

Made early telescopic observations of the Moon and sunspots and applied mathematics to ballistics and navigation.

people.biography: Galileo taught in Pisa and Padua before serving the Tuscan court. He combined measurement and mathematical reasoning in studies of motion and used improved telescopes to observe the sky. Tried for supporting Earth's motion, he nevertheless completed major work on mechanics in his later years.
contributions: Established quantitative relationships for falling bodies and uniformly accelerated motion and investigated projectile trajectories.
Advanced mechanics through discussions of inertia and relative motion.
Observed Jupiter's satellites and the phases of Venus, providing important evidence for a changed view of the heavens.

portrait.description: Galileo Galilei (1564-1642) A half-length portrait, in old age, of the Italian mathematician, philosopher and astronomer, who was appointed court mathematician to the Medici dukes of Tuscany at Florence in 1610. He is dressed in black, wears a white beard and is seated in a chair holding a telescope in his right hand. His left hand rests on the arm of the chair and he wears a ring with a clear stone on his fourth finger. He faces forward towards the viewer. Galileo, though not first inventor of the refracting telescope in 1609, enhanced its power, which enabled him to see that the Moon had mountains and that Jupiter had satellites. His championship of the Copernican (Sun-centred) planetary system brought him into serious conflict with the Roman Catholic church, which forced him to make a public recantation and put him under restriction in later life, as noted by the poet John Milton, who met him in Florence in 1638 and recorded in his 'Areopagitica': 'There it was I found the famous Galileo, grown old, a prisoner to the Inquisition for thinking in astronomy otherwise than the Franciscan and Dominican licensers thought.' The artist was a Flemish painter and draughtsman who worked in Florence as court painter to the Medici. He was considered the foremost portrait painter in Italy, with a strong interest in Venetian Renaissance art. This is one of the last portraits of Galileo and several versions and/or copies were made. With Hooke and others, he used improved air pumps to investigate gases. He promoted repeatable experiments and mechanical explanations of nature and strongly influenced experimental traditions in chemistry and physics.
contributions: Established the approximate inverse relationship between pressure and volume for a fixed quantity of gas at constant temperature.
Used air pumps to investigate combustion, respiration and sound propagation, advancing gas and vacuum experiments.

people.biography: Huygens was a Dutch mathematician, physicist and astronomer who worked at the royal academy in Paris before returning to the Netherlands. Investigated elastic collisions and the relation for centrifugal effects in circular motion.

Improved air pumps, microscopes and timekeeping devices, advancing experimental measurement.
Contributed to discussions of gravitation, orbital motion and optics.

people.biography: Dalton was an English chemist, physicist and weather observer from a Quaker family in Cumberland who later taught and researched in Manchester. Long-term meteorological records and gas studies informed his quantitative atomic theory. His investigation of his own colour vision also became historically influential.
contributions: Developed modern chemical atomic theory by relating composition to the relative masses of atoms.
Formulated the law of partial pressures and investigated gases and vapours.
Systematically studied colour-vision deficiency, contributing to scientific investigation of vision.
notes: Sources differ between 5 and 6 September; the Science Museum gives approximately 6 September.

Opened experimental research on thermoelectric conversion, providing a basis for thermocouples and thermoelectric devices.

Proposed a trichromatic account of colour vision, connecting optics to visual physiology.

people.biography: Avogadro was an Italian scholar initially trained in law who turned to natural science and taught physics in Turin. contributions: Proposed that equal gas volumes at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
Used molecular ideas to interpret combining gas volumes and relative molecular masses, supporting molecular theory and atomic-weight determination.

The Dulong–Petit law is approximate in an appropriate temperature range and fails in conditions including sufficiently low temperatures.

portrait.description: Since coming to IBM Research in 1972, Dr. Bennett has worked on various aspects of the relation between physics and information. In 1973, building on the work of IBM's Rolf Landauer, he showed that general-purpose computation can be performed by a logically and thermodynamically reversible apparatus, which can operate with arbitrarily little energy dissipation per step because it avoids throwing away information about past logical states. In 1982 he proposed a reinterpretation of Maxwell's demon, attributing its inability to break the second law to the thermodynamic cost of destroying, rather than acquiring, information. In collaboration with Gilles Brassard of the University of Montreal, he developed a practical system of quantum cryptography, allowing secure communication between parties who share no secret information initially, based on the uncertainty principle instead of usual computational assumptions such as the difficulty of factoring. In 1989 with the help of John Smolin, he built a working demonstration. In 1993 Dr. Bennett and Dr. Brassard, in collaboration with Claude Crepeau, Richard Jozsa, Asher Peres, and William Wootters, discovered "quantum teleportation," an effect in which the complete information in an unknown quantum state is decomposed into purely classical information and purely non-classical Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) correlations, sent through two separate channels, and later reassembled in a new location to produce an exact replica of the original quantum state that was destroyed in the sending process. contributions: Proposed large extra dimensions with Dimopoulos and Dvali.
Contributed to little-Higgs and split-supersymmetry models.
Developed geometric scattering-amplitude methods and the amplituhedron programme.

people.biography: A German experimental physicist trained in Hänsch's group, Bloch worked in Mainz, Munich, and the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics. He uses ultracold atoms in optical lattices to build controllable many-body quantum simulators.
contributions: Helped realize a superfluid-to-Mott-insulator quantum transition.
Developed control and imaging of optical-lattice quantum gases.
Simulated strongly correlated many-body models with ultracold atoms.

people.biography: A South African-born theorist who worked in Canada and the United States, Pretorius joined Princeton. His numerical studies of Einstein's equations overcame central obstacles to simulating merging black holes.
contributions: Produced an early stable simulation of binary-black-hole inspiral and merger.
Developed generalized-harmonic and numerical-relativity techniques.
Investigated strong-gravity dynamics and gravitational-wave generation.

people.biography: Konstantin Novoselov was born in Nizhny Tagil, Russia and conducted research in condensed-matter physics and two-dimensional materials. Nobel records list University of Manchester as the affiliation at the time of the award. They isolated and experimentally investigated graphene. They were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010.
contributions: Isolated and experimentally investigated graphene
Revealed distinctive electronic and quantum-transport properties of a two-dimensional carbon material
